prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 time-reversal-invariant topological insulator, and for the first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall state

statement.case_for: I keep B030 as a single-part prize with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. After round 1 the choice is really between B030 and B021, and I weigh them on the same three points: whether the discovery is settled, whether the credit can be written down, and whether a recent prize overlaps. B030 is settled. The Z2 classification and the quantum spin Hall proposal date from 2005, the HgTe observation from 2007, and nearly two decades of independent work in many materials have not changed the interpretation. It also gave the field a general organising principle, time-reversal-invariant topological insulators and their protected edge states, which fed into 3D materials, topological photonics and superconducting platforms. The credit has a defensible core: the prediction is Kane and Mele together, and the first observation is Molenkamp's group. I am moving from the opening position only in how I word the citation. It should name the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 topological insulator as predicted and then observed, and should not claim all of topological insulator physics.
statement.case_against: The attribution is the real weakness and I will not hide it. The Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal pointed the experiment to HgTe, and Hasan's 3D observations are a separate, weighty line, so any three names leave out a legitimate contributor. Five members also raise the 2016 prize on topological phases and phase transitions as a reason for caution. B021 has the stronger opening support, with three first places, and it is the second choice of most of the committee. A prize this year for B030 would therefore be a choice to favour maturity and a stable interpretation over a younger and more widely preferred case. If the committee is not persuaded that the credit can be defended, the honest outcome is B021, not a diluted B030.

responses.point: Johansson said he would revisit B030 if colleagues could show that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang role is adequately covered by the three-name credit, and Lindroth and Olsson raise the same attribution concern.
responses.response: My answer is that the credit should follow what each contribution established. Kane and Mele proposed the effect and the Z2 invariant and were the first to say that a time-reversal-invariant insulator has protected edge states. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made a concrete, important and correct material prediction, but it was a prediction for a system whose phenomenon had already been proposed. Molenkamp's group then did the decisive observation. That ordering is the reason to credit prediction and first observation in the citation, and it means BHZ is a real omission in the sense of a three-name limit, not a misattribution of the discovery. Nothing in this changes if the committee prefers a different trio; I only say that a trio without Mele would be harder to defend than the one I propose. I accept that this does not remove the objection, and that Johansson may weigh the omission more heavily than I do.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B021, with MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Bistritzer, as a prediction-then-discovery chain with a clean split and a timely recognition, and treats the unsettled mechanism as acceptable for a platform prize.
responses.response: I agree with most of the structure of that argument, and I regard B021 as the strongest alternative and a result I could support. Where I still differ is the standard for maturity. The Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction and the 2018 observation of correlated and superconducting states are secure as phenomenology. What is not secure is what the correlated phases are, and a citation limited to the flat bands and observed phases would honour a platform whose physical interpretation may still move. I do not say that disqualifies it; Eriksson is right that a platform prize does not need a mechanism. I say that a committee that can choose between a settled case and a younger one has a reason to take the settled one first. I also note that Eriksson himself lists B030 as an alternative, so on scientific standing we do not disagree.

responses.point: Olsson raises the 2016 prize as having already honoured topological phases and argues that B021 has a tighter theory-plus-experiment split, while accepting that the discovery of the B021 phases is not in doubt.
responses.response: The 2016 point deserves a direct answer because it was raised by five members. Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz were honoured for topological phase transitions and for topological phases in the integer quantum Hall setting and in one-dimensional chains. That is topology in systems with broken time-reversal symmetry or in low dimensions. The Kane-Mele quantum spin Hall effect is a new class, protected by time-reversal symmetry and carried by helical edge states without a magnetic field, and it led to the experimental programme in HgTe and later 3D materials. I think a citation worded around that distinction answers the overlap objection, though I accept it will not satisfy someone who thinks one topology prize in a decade is enough. On her second point, the B021 split is tighter, and I grant that.

responses.point: Kroll presses for B024 with Katori and Ye, with a decade of independent confirmation, concrete use in geodesy and constants tests, and the cleanest two-name credit, and asks how the committee should weigh a measurement achievement against a new-state-of-matter achievement.
responses.response: Kroll's case is strong, and I agree that the credit is simpler than for anything else on the list. I still place a conceptual discovery ahead of a measurement achievement this year, but I treat this as a difference of weighting and not as a reason against B024. What would move me is the payoff he himself says has not yet arrived: a redefinition of the second or a new-physics limit would make the clock case look like a completed chapter, and I would then expect to favour it. For this year I have therefore moved B024 into my alternatives in place of B033. I would not support a two-part prize that pairs B030 with B024, because it would use all three names on two parts and dilute both citations.

responses.point: Mehlig opened with Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan for B030 and in round 1 ranks B021 first, while conceding that eight years is short and that any three names on B030 leave out someone.
responses.response: I take his three-name alternative seriously and have thought about whether it would be more defensible than mine. It would give the committee an experimental credit for both the 2D and 3D discoveries, which is attractive. But it would cut the theory credit in half, because Kane and Mele wrote the founding papers together and the Z2 classification is the idea that makes 3D topological insulators a coherent subject at all. I would keep Mele. I also agree with his concession on maturity, and I think it carries weight: it is the one point where B021 is clearly behind, and it is the reason I stay with B030. If the committee instead decides to honour the 3D materials, I would want that as a separate achievement, not a swap inside this one.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts leaving out Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and Hasan, or prefers to treat the credit problem as a reason to choose B021 this year.
Whether the 2016 topology prize is read as covering this area or as a separate discovery with time-reversal symmetry protection.

Whether the unsettled interpretation of the correlated phases in twisted bilayer graphene is disqualifying for B021 or normal for a young field; my own view is that it is a reason to wait, not a reason to refuse.
I rely on my own recollection of the priority history and have not verified the chronology against primary sources in this exercise.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile. My documented connections are my PhD supervisor David Gross, my early mentor Hector Rubinstein, my co-author Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theoretical-physics group, and none of them is a credited name on any shortlisted ballot. As a string theorist I have no direct expertise in the condensed-matter and atomic-physics fields that dominate the shortlist and I rely on the written record and my colleagues for those judgments. As Secretary I note that this statement is a position, not a procedural ruling.
